Elle veut, elle veut explore le masculin: Elle veut, elle veut explores masculinism among young people, revealing harassment and cyberbullying while encouraging dialogue and change.

<strong>Nous sommes le 31 mars, et c’est: It’s March 31, and it’s launch night at La Converse. The mood is festive, in stark contrast to the seriousness of the subject of the podcast taking centre stage. Spanning four episodes, Elle veut, elle veut takes stock of masculinism. Through testimonies, conversations and analysis, it dives into what young people are living through, in order to open a dialogue about relationships and, perhaps even, to find solutions to change the dynamics between men and women.
Les animatrices et instigatrices du proj: The hosts and driving forces behind the project are Melissa, Abigail, Razane and Malika – all four racialized Montrealers in their early twenties. Until recently, they carried the project anonymously, which says a lot about the backlash such a subject can provoke.
« Ça a commencé au cégep avec des débats: “It started at CEGEP with group debates: the girls, the guys,” says Razane. Following Momo’s intervention, a meeting took place between the students and Lela Savic, La Converse’s editor-in-chief. The effect was immediate. “We ended up getting off our chests what we had been holding in, what we saw at school, and how many girls didn’t feel comfortable enough in the hallways, in certain specific places at school. We had a lot to say, but nobody to listen,” Razane continues.
« Elles m’ont parlé de ce qu’elles viven: “They told me about what they’re going through,” says Lela. The effect of these conversations was such that the editor-in-chief felt it necessary to mobilize the resources needed to carry out an initiative with these young women, from a journalistic perspective.
Pour les quatre journalistes en herbe, i: For the four budding journalists, it is a first taste of the profession. “I really liked our conversations at CEGEP, and I wanted to know more about masculinism because it’s so broad,” explains Abigail. “I had the chance to speak publicly, because not every girl can do that freely,” she continues, noting that she is trembling with nervousness, being introverted by nature. “Thanks to this podcast, I was able to carry the voices of girls who couldn’t. It’s a success.”
« Je suis très heureuse d’avoir pu démys: “I’m very happy to have been able to demystify some things,” adds Melissa about the podcast. “It’s important to represent what we go through, the realities we have. I also wanted to share what I’ve experienced in the podcast,” Malika continues.
Les apprenties journalistes ont couvert: The apprentice journalists covered sensitive subjects: the harassment, bullying and attacks endured by girls and women. They had to find and collect testimonies from girls, sometimes very young, who were willing to speak on the mic. “They did groundwork to see how it plays out. These are conversations we mostly have among adults, but when you see it’s something that starts in elementary school, it was quite shocking to hear,” explains Lela Savic.
C’est ce que les journalistes en herbe o: That’s what the budding journalists were able to observe in the field. “From a very young age, [girls] already feel pressure. If they want to play with a little boy, he might tell them: ‘Don’t play with me.’ There’s a separation in the classroom: girls on one side, boys on the other. There’s so much work to do,” says Melissa.
Devant un enjeu aussi sensible, les anim: Faced with such a sensitive issue, the hosts first had to work under the cover of anonymity, all the while keeping in mind that those who speak out also expose themselves. “There’s a certain fear: Montréal is small, and it’s easy to identify people,” laments Malika. “As a woman, you go through a lot of things, but you don’t necessarily want people to know what you’re going through,” says Razane.
Cette dernière a été particulièrement ma: Razane was particularly struck by “confession accounts”: a real scourge on social media, where anonymous posts discredit female students. “At one school, it went to extremes! Girls were harassed for days, for weeks, until the account was shutdown,” Razane reports.
Difficile de ne pas être affectée, indiq: It’s hard not to be affected, she says, when you watch a student get harassed “morning, noon and night” on social media. “Seeing the direct impact of social media on this girl… I didn’t know her from Adam, and yet I wanted to comfort her, but I couldn’t, because it was part of the job,” she says.
Razane fait également remarquer que la g: Razane also points out that the seriousness of this kind of situation is downplayed by those who experience it and by the people around them. “‘I went for a walk, and I got called a slut.’ It’s become so normal in their reality.” And the worst part of all this, Razane continues, is that the girls are all afraid of ending up in the same situation if they help a girl who is subjected to such remarks.
En parlant des conséquences de ce genre: Speaking about the consequences of this kind of behaviour, Malika adds that after the bullying episode mentioned above, the student said she no longer wanted to go to school – which could only jeopardize her academic path. The young journalist describes the pressure she experienced as a student at Cégep de Maisonneuve.
« Si tu portais des leggins, tu étais co: “If you wore leggings, you were considered a slut. After my gym class, I would change and put on jeans or sweatpants,” she remembers. She goes on to describe other situations. “There was a bench where there were always guys. You were just walking by and they’d point at you, make comments.” Social media means the harassment continues outside the school walls. “You’re at home, minding your own business, and someone calls you a slut. You did nothing. Just because you have a public account. Or else, someone takes a picture of you on the street and sends it to a groupchat. You’re going to change the way you are so you don’t get targeted. It’s not normal,” Malika says.
Pour sa part, Melissa a dû agir à titre:
For her part, Melissa had to act as a mediator after some of the testimonies. “It was stronger than me; it really got to me. I hadn’t realized the scale, the seriousness of this situation. Wow, all of this is happening in the place we go to every day? I was a bit shocked,” she says.

The young host believes that cyberbullying is especially underestimated. She relays the words of young girls: “Getting called every name in the book? That’s just how it is. Anyway, what do you want me to do? Even if I talk about it, it won’t change anything.” “You take it on yourself and you say, ‘It’s no big deal,’ but really, it’s a huge deal,” she believes.
Melissa souligne que des mesures ont heu: Melissa points out that measures have fortunately been taken and that one of the podcast’s episodes is about this. However, she fears it isn’t enough. “In our communities, I think we really don’t talk about it enough. It’s still taboo,” she says. “I’d like to be able to do more than a podcast.”
Sam Chourot étudiant à la maîtrise en sc: Sam Chourot, master’s student in political science specializing in intersectional masculinities.
C’est loin d’être le seul défi qu’ont dû: That is far from the only challenge the journalists had to face while making the podcast. As Lela points out, “you can’t talk about this subject without talking to men.” One episode of Elle veut, elle veut is therefore devoted to their testimonies.
« Il y a un épisode où on a parlé avec l: “There’s an episode where we talked with the boys, and it was a very sensitive and emotional moment. Some of the answers were hurtful,” Razane confides.
« Dans une perspective de journalisme, i: “From a journalistic perspective, you have to be neutral. When you’re faced with comments that, normally, you wouldn’t let slide, you have to stay neutral, be professional, set aside your biases,” adds her colleague Malika. “When we were facing the guys and could see it clashed with how we think, it was hard.”
Malgré ce qu’on ressent au fond de soi,: Despite what you feel deep down, you have to dig. “It’s important to set aside biases, because it lets you understand where these ways of thinking come from in these guys, and even in girls sometimes,” she says, thinking back on those exchanges.
Pour cause, les façons de penser peuvent: Indeed, ways of thinking can change, and the journalists have witnessed it. “I was in episode 3. I talked about toxicity among men and among women. Looking back, I think women go through a lot more than we think, and it’s thanks to this kind of project that a man can change, myself first and foremost,” says a listener, thanking the hosts for their work.
La série se termine par des analyses d’e: The series ends with expert analysis. Melissa now hopes to go beyond the podcast. “The project opens doors for further research. I’d like to understand a bit more where all this comes from, and look for solutions.”
Elle veut, elle veut : un balado sur le: Elle veut, elle veut: a podcast on masculinism, harassment and the daily lives of young girls”
Le balado “Elle veut, elle veut” explore: The podcast “Elle veut, elle veut” explores masculinism, harassment and the pressures experienced by young girls in Montréal. Through testimonies, analysis and conversations with young people and experts, this podcast sheds light on cyberbullying, dynamics between men and women, and realities that are often rendered invisible in schools and on social media. An essential series for understanding and thinking about solutions for a safer, more equitable daily life for young people.
